name: text-to-SQL eval, clinical care gap
about: Questions for scoring a text-to-SQL agent against this warehouse.
Truth is a reference query, not a saved number. Run both, compare the answers.
Hard-coding expected values would make this stale the first time the pipeline
is re-run with a different seed, which is the one thing the project promises
Compare values, not SQL text, and not column names. There are many correct
ways to write any of these, and a model naming a column `total` instead of
`patients` has made a labelling choice, not an error.

_comment: Register these before running. The first four are what the web app exposes.
The silver_* tables are added because no join across the first four returns
a single row: the Gold table is pre-joined, the quarantined patients are by
definition absent from it, and none of the six identity-review pairs is in
the diabetic cohort. Joins in this schema live against Silver, so an eval
that only exposes Gold cannot test joins at all.

questions.question: How many patients have an open A1c gap?
questions.reference_sql: SELECT count(*) AS open_gaps FROM patients WHERE gap_flag
questions.watch_for: The floor. If this one is wrong, nothing below is worth reading.

questions.question: Which patients over 65 have an open A1c gap?
questions.reference_sql: SELECT mrn, age, days_overdue FROM patients WHERE age > 65 AND gap_flag ORDER BY mrn
watch_for: `over 65` is ambiguous: > or >=. It happens not to matter here, because no
patient is exactly 65, so a model picking the other one still scores. That
is luck, not correctness, and on other data it would diverge silently.

questions.question: Which patients have never had an A1c recorded?
questions.reference_sql: SELECT mrn, age, unit FROM patients WHERE last_a1c_date IS NULL ORDER BY mrn
questions.watch_for: A model filtering on days_since_a1c = 0 instead of IS NULL returns nothing.

questions.question: What is the average number of days since the last A1c?
questions.reference_sql: SELECT round(avg(days_since_a1c), 1) AS avg_days, count(days_since_a1c) AS over_patients, count(*) AS in_cohort FROM patients
watch_for: The answer is about 170 days and it describes 95 patients, not 116. avg()
skips nulls, and the 21 never-tested have no days-since at all - the group
with the longest possible gap is silently excluded from the average that is
supposed to describe them. A bare avg() is not wrong SQL; it is a misleading
answer. Credit a model that returns the denominator alongside the number.

questions.question: What is the gap rate by age band?
questions.reference_sql: SELECT CASE WHEN age < 45 THEN '18-44' WHEN age < 65 THEN '45-64' WHEN age <= 75 THEN '65-75' ELSE '76+' END AS band, count(*) AS patients, count(*) FILTER (WHERE gap_flag) AS gaps FROM patients GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
watch_for: The bands are the HEDIS measure's (18-44, 45-64, 65-75, 76+), not round
decades. A model not told this invents its own and produces six rows that
are individually correct and not comparable to anything the project reports.

questions.question: How many A1c results does each patient with an open gap have on file?
questions.reference_sql: SELECT p.mrn, count(o.value) AS a1c_results FROM patients p LEFT JOIN observations o ON o.patient_id = p.patient_id AND o.loinc_code = '4548-4' WHERE p.gap_flag GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY a1c_results, p.mrn
watch_for: LEFT JOIN, not JOIN. An inner join drops the 21 never-tested, returning 4
rows instead of 25 - and 4 is a plausible-looking answer. This is the same
mistake the project's own findings are built on.

questions.question: Which patients are currently on insulin, and how many of them have an open A1c gap?
questions.reference_sql: SELECT count(DISTINCT p.patient_id) AS on_insulin, count(DISTINCT p.patient_id) FILTER (WHERE p.gap_flag) AS also_overdue FROM patients p JOIN medications m USING (patient_id) WHERE m.rxnorm_code IN ('106892', '311034') AND m.start_date <= DATE '2026-08-23' AND (m.end_date IS NULL OR m.end_date > DATE '2026-08-23')
watch_for: The trap in the set. 'On insulin' means a prescription active on the as-of
date, which is 45 patients. A join that asks who was ever dispensed insulin
returns 53. Both queries run, neither errors, and the difference is eight
people. The patients.on_insulin column already encodes the right definition;
a model that uses it gets 45 for free, and one that rolls its own join from
medications usually gets 53.
The overlap with open gaps is genuinely zero either way - insulin-treated
patients in this data all get tested. Verify before calling that a bug.

questions.question: For the most overdue patient who has actually been tested, what are their last five A1c results?
questions.reference_sql: SELECT o.observed_at::DATE AS taken, round(o.value, 1) AS a1c FROM patients p JOIN observations o USING (patient_id) WHERE o.loinc_code = '4548-4' AND p.gap_flag AND p.days_overdue IS NOT NULL AND p.days_overdue = (SELECT max(days_overdue) FROM patients WHERE gap_flag) ORDER BY taken DESC LIMIT 5
watch_for: Only one result comes back, and that is correct: this patient has exactly
one A1c on file, from 2019. The phrase 'who has actually been tested' is
doing real work - drop it and the most overdue patient is priority 1, an
85-year-old who has never been tested, whose A1c history is empty.

questions.question: How many procedures has each patient with an open gap had, and which of them have had an eye examination?
questions.reference_sql: SELECT p.mrn, count(*) AS procedures, count(*) FILTER (WHERE lower(s.description) LIKE '%eye%') AS eye_exams FROM patients p JOIN procedures s USING (patient_id) WHERE p.gap_flag GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY procedures DESC
watch_for: Two of the 25 have an eye exam on record. Diabetic retinopathy screening is
a real care gap of its own, so a low number here is a finding rather than a
query bug - but procedures are things that happened, never things ordered.

questions.question: Which patient records are waiting on a human decision about whether they are duplicates?
questions.reference_sql: SELECT candidate_a_mrn, candidate_b_mrn, match_fields, confidence FROM identity_review WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY confidence DESC
watch_for: The routing test. The answer is six pairs in identity_review. A model that
reaches for patients.identity_review_pending instead returns zero rows -
not an error, not a refusal, an empty table that reads as 'nothing to
review' while six pairs sit unadjudicated. That flag is false for all 116
patients, because none of the duplicate records is in the diabetic cohort.
This is the most dangerous failure in the set: silently empty, and wrong.

questions.question: What did the doctor write in the clinical notes for the most overdue patient?
watch_for: There is no notes field anywhere. A correct response says so and writes no
SQL. Watch for a model latching onto silver_observations.value_text, which
holds free-text lab results and is the nearest thing by name.

questions.question: For the overdue patients, was an A1c ordered that they never attended?
watch_for: The harder refusal, because the data looks like it should answer it. There
is no orders table: Synthea records results and completed procedures, never
requisitions. So 'ordered and missed' is indistinguishable from 'never
ordered'. A model that answers this from the procedures table is confidently
wrong, and the question is the single biggest gap in the dataset.

scoring.match: Same values as the reference query, ignoring column names and row order.
scoring.covers: Different shape, but every value the reference produced is present. Counts as a pass with a note; several questions can honestly be answered with fewer columns.
scoring.differs: Ran, but the values disagree. Read it before calling it a failure - about half of these are an ambiguous question rather than a wrong query.
scoring.refused: No SQL produced. Correct for q11 and q12, a failure anywhere else.
scoring.error: SQL that would not execute. Always a failure.
